claim_verdicts.source: GitHub Docs: .../proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests and .../creating-a-pull-request (fetched 2026-09-22)
claim_verdicts.evidence: "Pull requests are proposals to merge code changes into a project." And on creating one: "Use the base branch dropdown menu to select the branch where you want to merge your changes. Then, use the compare branch dropdown menu to choose the topic branch where you made your changes." Merging is a separate act (the same pages describe a merge box and state "Draft pull requests cannot be merged"). Caveat: docs.github.com appears in versions.yaml only under github_actions — see the version issue.

claim_verdicts.source: https://git-scm.com/docs (command index; git pinned at 2.46 in versions.yaml), fetched 2026-09-22
claim_verdicts.evidence: The Git command index lists 79 commands, including branch, merge, diff, and request-pull (under "Email", the mail-based way to ask a maintainer to pull). There is no command for a pull request page, review comments or approval: Git ships the branch and the merge, and nothing that holds comments or an approval. The page carrying those comes from the hosting service.

claim_verdicts.source: none — no doc root in content/versions.yaml covers the purposes of code review
claim_verdicts.evidence: Tried git-scm.com/docs and the GitHub Docs pull-request pages; neither states why review exists. GitHub Docs says only "A pull request brings together the context reviewers need to understand a change", which is not the three-purpose claim. The three ends come from outline item 1 of the lesson entry. Nothing contradicts them; there is no source for them either, and the lesson states them flatly ("three things come out of it").

claim_verdicts.source: GitHub Docs: about-protected-branches and about-pull-request-reviews (fetched 2026-09-22)
claim_verdicts.evidence: First half holds: administrators "can require that all pull requests receive a specific number of approving reviews before someone merges the pull request into a protected branch." Second half too strong: the review states are "Comment — Leaves general feedback without explicitly approving or requesting changes", "Approve — Signals that the changes are ready to merge", "Request changes — Flags feedback that the author should address before merging". The service tells those apart; only the single comment carries no grade.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: The grades are plain text: a hosting service can require an approval before a merge, and a reviewer can mark a whole review as still needing changes, but on a single comment the grade means nothing to the service; the team is what makes it mean something.

claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang docs/team/review-comments-examples.md @ stage-0 (git show stage-0:...) lines 7-9, 14-16, 31
claim_verdicts.evidence: The third comment asks rather than asserts ("Vì sao chỗ này bắt `Exception` chứ không bắt riêng `InvalidOperationException`?") and the first ends "hay mình hiểu sai tiêu chí?" — the reviewer allowing that they misread. Line 31 puts the answer on the author: "Trả lời từng nhận xét, kể cả nhận xét bạn không đồng ý." Both halves of the claim are in the file.

claim_verdicts.source: GitHub Docs: .../reviewing-changes-in-pull-requests/about-pull-request-reviews (fetched 2026-09-22)
claim_verdicts.evidence: "Approve — Signals that the changes are ready to merge." An approval says the change may merge, not that it cannot be improved; no document ties approval to an absence of possible improvement. The second half of the claim (a held change waits while its branch collects conflicts) is the lesson's illustration, not a documented fact, and the lesson keeps it as "You notice this when…".

claim_verdicts.source: definitional
claim_verdicts.evidence: Tautological once a pull request is defined: the description is written by whoever opens the request, and a reviewer who cannot read why the change exists has only the diff left to infer it from. Nothing on the GitHub Docs pull-request pages I opened contradicts it; they say a pull request "brings together the context reviewers need to understand a change".

claim_verdicts.source: GitHub Docs: .../proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/creating-a-pull-request (fetched 2026-09-22)
claim_verdicts.evidence: "After you open your pull request, you can continue changing files by adding new commits to your head branch." Commits pushed to the head branch after the request is open belong to the same pull request, so the request follows the branch rather than a fixed set of commits. Same source caveat as claim 10: the product is not pinned in versions.yaml.

claim_verdicts.source: none
claim_verdicts.evidence: Tried git-scm.com/docs and the GitHub Docs review pages; neither addresses how fast a junior picks up a team's unwritten standards, and no measurement is available here. The claim is a comparison ("sooner than one who only receives review") taken from outline item 4 and stated in the lesson as a consequence ("which is why…"). Not contradicted, not evidenced.

issues.quote: a hosting service can require an approval before a merge, but cannot tell a must-fix from a suggestion; the team does that
issues.text: Too strong, and the documentation contradicts the second half at review level. GitHub Docs lists three review states, among them "Request changes — Flags feedback that the author should address before merging" against "Comment — Leaves general feedback without explicitly approving or requesting changes". The service does distinguish a review that must be addressed from one that need not; what it cannot grade is the single line comment.
issues.fix: Replace the sentence with: "The grades are plain text: a hosting service can require an approval before a merge, and a reviewer can mark a whole review as still needing changes, but on a single comment the grade means nothing to the service; the team is what makes it mean something." No new term is introduced.

issues.quote: the comments this team left on an earlier pull request, a teammate's change merged before you joined that added order cancelling on the code you now touch
issues.text: Unlisted claim: the note says only "Các nhận xét dưới đây đều lấy từ pull request thêm chức năng hủy đơn" (line 3). Nothing in the file says the change was a teammate's, that it merged, or that it happened before the reader joined. Claim 1 in the ledger covers the provenance sentence and none of these three additions.
issues.fix: Cut to "the comments this team left on an earlier pull request, the one that added order cancelling on the code you now touch", or keep the framing and add a claim to .meta.json marking it as scenario, not as a statement about the file.

issues.quote: A reviewer then reads that diff, and three things come out of it.
issues.text: Claim 12 (the three purposes) and claim 20 (a junior who reviews meets the standard sooner) are asserted flatly and cannot be sourced from any docs root in versions.yaml — both are marked unverified above. Section 6 adds a third, unlisted ranking: "the cheapest comment in the note is a question".
issues.fix: Attribute instead of asserting: "Teams that review give three reasons for it" in section 4, and in section 6 "the lightest comment in the note is a question" (a fact about the grades the lesson defines). Add "cheapest/lightest comment" to the claims ledger.

issues.text: Claims 10, 13 and 19 are behaviours of a repository hosting service, not of Git. The only source that settles them is docs.github.com, which appears in content/versions.yaml only under the key github_actions whose docs root is https://docs.github.com/actions; the product whose behaviour the lesson asserts is pinned nowhere. Verified above against GitHub Docs, but outside the pinned root.
issues.fix: Ask the owner to add a `github` key to content/versions.yaml (docs: https://docs.github.com/, checked date), then put it in versions_used and give claims 10, 13, 19 that version_key. Until that is approved, record in .meta.json open_questions that these three were verified against GitHub Docs only, outside the pinned root.

issues.quote: the cancel-order story's criterion 3, which the comment reads as allowing cancellation only from `new`

The lesson's hedge carries the whole load; a reader who opens the story file finds the gap unexplained, and section 7 repeats the comment's reading in the suggested answer.

junior.reviewer: claude-opus-5 (junior reader simulation, prompt 05, fresh pass over the current text; known_vocab = 47 terms through definition-of-done, lesson vocab: code-review, pull-request; prereq input: good-commits and reading-code five-line summaries only)

issues.text: Step 1 tells me to cover the right-hand column of the table of bad comments, but the lesson never shows that table. Section 5 retells the four bad comments in prose with the reason already attached to each. With only the lesson in front of me - which the step says is enough - there is no column to cover and the answers are already given, so the exercise has nothing left to test.
issues.fix: Replace 'cover the right-hand column of the table of bad comments' with 'take the four bad comments as section 5 lists them and ignore the reason the lesson gives beside each'.
issues.quote: Open `docs/team/review-comments-examples.md` (any copy will do: the lesson quotes every line you need) and cover the right-hand column of the table of bad comments.

issues.text: Step 1 asks for two things about each of four comments (the missing clause and the grade it should have carried), plus a special answer for 'OK.', and step 2 then asks for a full rewrite. That is nine written answers; I would not finish in three minutes.
issues.fix: Cut step 1 to two of the four bad comments, keeping 'OK.' as the second, and leave step 2 as it is.

issues.text: I know what a conflict is (both sides changed the same region of a file), but nothing here says why a branch that is only waiting starts collecting them. I had to guess that teammates keep merging into the target branch meanwhile. The same picture comes back in quiz q6, so I guessed twice.
issues.fix: Extend the sentence to '... waits three days over one name while teammates merge their own changes into the target branch and the branch collects conflicts'.
issues.quote: You notice this when a pull request waits three days over one name while the branch collects conflicts.

issues.text: 'The third' made me stop and count backwards. Only the acceptance criteria are marked 'first'; the Definition of Done is never called second, so I had to reread the previous sentence to work out which three documents are being counted.
issues.fix: Replace 'This note itself is the third' with 'This note is the third of those written-down standards'.
issues.quote: This note itself is the third: it fixes how a comment is phrased.

issues.text: I read this sentence three times. Two appositives stack up before the colon, and 'that added order cancelling' looks at first as if it attaches to 'you joined' rather than to the teammate's change. It is the second sentence of the lesson's only story, so it is a bad place to lose the reader.
issues.fix: Split it: 'It collects the comments this team left on an earlier pull request: a teammate's change, merged before you joined, that added order cancelling to the code you now touch. Four comments it calls good, then a table of four it calls bad with the reason beside each.'
issues.quote: It collects the comments this team left on an earlier pull request, a teammate's change merged before you joined that added order cancelling on the code you now touch: four it calls good, then a table of four it calls bad with the reason beside each.

issues.text: 'diff' is a new word for me and the lesson leans on it everywhere afterwards: the diagram, sections 4 and 5, and four quiz questions. It is explained, but only inside an em-dash of the pull request bullet, so on first reading I took it as part of what a pull request is, not as a word I would need to hold on to.
issues.fix: Restructure the bullet so the gloss stands on its own: 'a pull request - a request to merge one branch into another. It carries the diff, every line the merge would change, and a place to write beside it.'
issues.quote: **pull request** — a request to merge one branch into another, carrying the diff — every line the merge would change — and a place to write beside it.

issues.text: Everything I have been taught about Git is local commands. This is the first time a page and a service appear, and the lesson never says how the repository comes to be on such a service or how I would reach that page, so I could not picture where I would actually be typing a comment.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after it: 'The team's repository has a copy on such a service, and the pull request is a page there that you open in a browser.'
issues.quote: Git gives you the branch and the merge; the page holding the diff, the comments and the approval comes from the service hosting the repository.

issues.text: LINQ is a name I have not met. The gloss 'another style, whichever style that is' is enough for the point being made (the comment gives no reason), but it reads as if the lesson itself does not know what LINQ is, which made me stop and wonder whether I was supposed to.
issues.fix: Change the gloss to '(rewrite it all in a different style - which style does not matter here, because the comment gives no reason)'.
issues.quote: "Đổi hết sang LINQ đi" (rewrite it all in another style, whichever style that is) is a preference with no reason and no grade.

issues.text: I do not know what `stage-0` is. 'the version this lesson reads' tells me it is a version of something, but not of what, so I could not tell whether it is something I have to fetch before the Try it step.
issues.fix: Expand the apposition to 'at `stage-0`, the version of the example repository this lesson reads'.
issues.quote: a note the repository keeps at `stage-0`, the version this lesson reads

issues.text: The two correct options are the only two that open with a grade word ('Must fix.', 'Question.'). I picked them off that pattern before reading the reasons, so the question did not test whether I know a good comment names a place and a reason.
issues.fix: Open one wrong option with a grade word as well, e.g. start option e with 'Suggestion.' - it still fails on having no reason beyond preference.
issues.quote: Move every check up to the top of the method; that is the way the rest of us lay one out.

issues.text: `order_items` does not appear anywhere in the lesson, so I stopped to ask whether it is a table, a class or a list I was supposed to remember. It does not change the answer, but it made me doubt I had read the lesson properly.
issues.fix: Replace `order_items` with a name the lesson uses, or with plain words: 'the total skips the last line of the order'.
issues.quote: Must fix. On line 87 the total skips the last row of `order_items`, so an order with two products bills for one.
